name: Dudu Miya
contribution: Dudu Miya, whose given name was Muhsinuddin Ahmad, succeeded his father Haji Shariatullah as head of the Faraizi movement in 1840. He shifted the movement toward organized agrarian mobilization, opposing illegal cesses and coercive practices associated with zamindars and European indigo planters in eastern Bengal.
context: Born in 1819 in the Madaripur area of greater Faridpur, Dudu Miya led rural communities during conflicts over rent, cultivation, local authority, and religious practice under Company rule. He revived panchayat-based arbitration and built a hierarchical khalifa network that connected village units to the movement's leadership at Bahadurpur.
impact: The Faraizi movement under Dudu Miya combined religious reform with social protection and agrarian politics. His claim that land rights should follow cultivation attracted peasants across religious and caste lines, while his lathial forces and parallel courts also brought the movement into open conflict with landlords, planters, and colonial authorities. He died in 1862, but the movement remained part of Bengal's history of rural resistance.
highlight: Faraizi leader who connected Islamic reform, peasant protection, and organized agrarian resistance in eastern Bengal.
seoTitle: Dudu Miya: Faraizi Movement and Peasant Resistance in Bengal
seoDescription: Learn about Dudu Miya, successor to Haji Shariatullah, and his role in turning the Faraizi movement into an organized peasant force in nineteenth-century Bengal.
shortAnswer: Dudu Miya was the nineteenth-century leader who turned the Faraizi movement into a major organized peasant and agrarian force in eastern Bengal.

faq.question: Who was Dudu Miya?
faq.answer: Dudu Miya, or Muhsinuddin Ahmad, was the son and successor of Faraizi founder Haji Shariatullah. He led the movement from 1840 until his death in 1862.

faq.question: How did Dudu Miya change the Faraizi movement?
faq.answer: He gave it a stronger agrarian and organizational character by protecting peasants from illegal exactions, using panchayat arbitration, and coordinating village communities through a khalifa network.
